title: Nuisance

definition.text: A common-law wrong where someone's activity causes offence, annoyance or harm to others, such as a smoking chimney or loud noise.

facts.text: A nuisance is public when it interferes with rights shared by everyone, such as public health and safety, and private when it affects specific people.
Landholders are entitled to quiet enjoyment of their land; a neighbour's smells, sounds or pollution crossing the boundary can ground a nuisance claim.
Nuisance is one of the oldest causes of action in the common law.
As nuisance suits became costly to settle, most places adopted zoning to say which activities are allowed where.
Modern environmental laws adapt the nuisance idea to harms that reach people far from the source.
Noise, water and light pollution are among the environmental harms treated as nuisances in law.

notes: Several sentences are flagged CITATION NEEDED (8b83812beaa9).

definition.text: The two ways courts deal with a nuisance: ordering payment of damages, or issuing an injunction to stop the activity.

facts.text: Under the old common law, damages were the only remedy; courts of equity later added the injunction.
The law and economics movement analyses which remedy is most efficient in each case.
In the Atlantic Cement case, a New York court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of obeying an injunction, since compliance would cost far more than the neighbours' harm.
In theory, permanent damages should equal the net present value of all future harm to the plaintiff.

definition.text: The question of whether someone who moves next to an existing nuisance can still complain about it.

facts.text: In English law, unlike US law, coming to the nuisance is no defence; the 1879 case Sturges v Bridgman still stands.
Many US states limit nuisance claims, for example with right-to-farm rules protecting agriculture from newcomers' complaints about smells.
Coase used Sturges v Bridgman, a noisy sweet-maker next to a quiet doctor, to illustrate his argument.

definition.text: A legal rule that makes a person responsible for harm caused by their activity even when they were not at fault.

facts.text: Someone who keeps something inherently dangerous is liable for resulting damage no matter how carefully it was guarded.
US courts have treated storing large amounts of flammable liquid in a city, noxious factory fumes in settled areas, and oil wells in populated places as ultrahazardous.
By making defendants pay regardless of fault, it pushes them to take every possible precaution.
An early example is Rylands v Fletcher: whoever keeps something on their land likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage.
After an environmental impact assessment, the polluter pays principle may be used to require strict liability or insurance for a project.
Strict liability in US aviation helped push small-aircraft production from 18,000 units a year in 1978 to a few hundred by 1993.

definition.text: Ronald Coase's 1960 law review article on the economic problem of externalities, such as pollution harming neighbours.

facts.text: Coase argued that with no costs of making deals, people would bargain their way to the most efficient use of resources whatever the starting legal rights.
Because real bargaining and information are costly, legal rules matter insofar as they give rights to whoever values them most.
Many useful deals never happen because of these transaction costs, such as sorting genuine claims from many neighbours or holdouts demanding too much.
Its lesson was that the burden should be on governments to show their interventions do more good than harm.
Its argument became the basis of what George Stigler labelled the Coase theorem.
It showed the Pigouvian tax is not the only path to dealing with externalities.
It founded the field of law and economics, is the most frequently cited work in legal scholarship, and was cited in Coase's 1991 Nobel Prize.

title: Reciprocal nature of harm

definition.text: Coase's idea that a nuisance is not simply one party's fault but a clash of two parties' interests, each of whom imposes a cost on the other.

facts.text: In Bryant v Lefever, a neighbour's new wall made a chimney smoke; Coase said the smoke was caused both by the wall-builder and the person lighting fires.
Coase concluded that the cost of exercising a right is always the loss suffered elsewhere.

notes: No page of its own; drawn from The Problem of Social Cost (lead and Summary). Passes the two-page test via Market failure/Coase theorem pages discussing the article.

title: Cheapest cost avoider
article: The Problem of Social Cost#Theoretical challenges

definition.text: The party able to prevent a harm at the lowest cost, to whom liability can efficiently be assigned when bargaining is hard.

facts.text: Guido Calabresi argued in The Costs of Accidents (1970) that it can still be efficient to hold wealth-producing companies liable.
When one factory's smoke harms many farms, the farmers struggle to organize, and some may free ride rather than pay their share.
The factory may know best how to cut harm, making it the cheapest avoider.

title: Marginal damage

definition.text: The extra harm done to others by one more unit of a polluting activity, also called the marginal external cost.

facts.text: Steel production causes marginal damages through pollution and other environmental effects.
Pigou argued for a tax equal to the marginal damage per unit to correct the externality.
A tax around 50% higher or lower than marginal damages still captures around three quarters of the welfare gain, so broad coverage matters more than precise measurement.
Weitzman showed that if marginal damages rise more steeply than abatement costs, quantity controls work better than price controls.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Internalizing externalities

definition.text: Making those who cause an external cost bear it themselves, so their private costs line up with the costs to society.

facts.text: Pigou proposed corrective taxes aimed at internalizing externalities by aligning private and social costs.
A corrective tax is one of the public remedies for internalizing externalities.
Carbon trading is a prime example of a shift toward internalizing externalities.
Pricing an externality at its marginal damage lets producers and consumers choose the cheapest way to cut emissions.
An older ecological economics critique questions whether internalizing externalities can really correct the current system.

contested_note: Ecological economists question whether internalizing externalities can correct market systems, while mainstream economists favour it.
notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Property rules and liability rules

definition.text: Legal rules, described by Calabresi and Melamed, under which a liability rule is a form of legalized private expropriation that can be used when transaction costs block voluntary trade.

facts.text: Calabresi and Melamed argue such liability rules can increase welfare when transaction costs are large.
In the Atlantic Cement nuisance case, a court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of being stopped by injunction.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; only one sentence (f808c970f9bf) states the idea; the property-rule half is not described in the sources (see gaps).

title: Transboundary pollution

definition.text: Pollution produced in one country that crosses borders and harms other places.

facts.text: Acid rain from sulfur dioxide became a major issue as it spread across borders.
Some countries pass their pollution to other places to clean up, prompting laws on holding countries liable for damage.
ASEAN ministers called in 1990 for harmonized transboundary pollution prevention, leading to a 2002 agreement on haze.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.
